outcome: No progress on the general characterization (Hasse's problem) of which algebraic number fields admit a power integral basis. Research since 26 January 2024 continues in the same vein as before that date: family-specific monogenity criteria (trinomials, quadrinomials, pure cubic/octic fields, sextic fields with a real quadratic subfield, polynomial compositions), none of which advance the general classification question.
summary: The bullet asks for a characterization of all algebraic number fields admitting a power (integral) basis — this is the classical problem attributed to Hasse, of deciding for which number fields the ring of integers is monogenic (Z_K = Z[α] for some α). This is a genuine 'characterize all X' question, so per §3.1 it moves only when a general characterization is proved, not when another special family is settled. I searched arXiv, Google Scholar-style web search, and read I. Gaál's 2024 survey 'Monogenity and Power Integral Bases: Recent Developments' (arXiv:2407.00374, published in Axioms 13(7):429, July 2024) which is the standard up-to-date digestion of this subfield. The survey opens by stating the classical problem and then, rather than presenting any general characterization, catalogs decades of incremental, family-by-family results (pure fields, trinomials, quadrinomials, sextic/octic fields, etc.), and its 'Further Research' section explicitly poses open questions about even restricted cases (e.g., quartic and quintic fields in general, or arbitrary trinomials of degree ≤9), confirming the general problem is unsolved and was treated as such as of mid-2024. I then searched specifically for post-January-2024 work: results include a 2025 paper on quadrinomial monogenic fields (Chatterjee/Kumar, Springer Research in Number Theory 2025, arXiv:2408.14117), 2025 work on pure/octic fields, sextic fields with real quadratic subfields (arXiv:2505.04293), polynomial compositions (arXiv:2606.09739), and pure number fields with non-squarefree discriminants (arXiv:2506.16496). Every one of these is scoped to a specific polynomial family or field type — each is a 'case' in the §3.1 sense (restricting the question to a class), not a step toward a general characterization, and none of the papers claims to advance the overall classification. None of these papers, nor any secondary source found, mentions any AI system (LLM, neural network, or other machine-learning method) being used in obtaining these results; the methods described throughout (Newton polygons, Dedekind's criterion, Thue/index-form equation solving, Baker-type bounds) are traditional computational algebraic number theory, implemented in systems like Magma, not AI. This matches the triage record's conclusion of verdict 'none', and I did not find grounds to disagree with it.
competing_reading: One could argue that the accumulation of many family-specific characterizations over the years constitutes incremental progress toward a full characterization, since it maps out where monogenicity criteria are understood. But per §3.1, a case is a restriction of the stated question, and it does not move the general 'characterize all fields' status forward in the sense the status field tracks — it would only count as `partial` if it settled a scoping question. Wikipedia's bullet asks for a characterization of 'all' fields, and no source treats any of these family results as contributing to that general characterization (rather than being isolated special cases), so I classify as `open` rather than `partial`. If a future reader believes even one of these family papers should count as `partial` progress (settling monogenicity for an entire infinite class, e.g. all pure octic fields), that is a defensible alternative reading, but it does not change the overall open status of the general characterization problem, nor introduce any AI involvement.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or survey that proposes and proves (or substantially narrows) a general arithmetic criterion applicable across number fields of all/most degrees for admitting a power integral basis — as opposed to a criterion tied to one polynomial shape or field family — would settle whether real progress on the general problem occurred. Absent that, the status remains open.
